dedupe_keys.name: hurricane induced power outage risk under climate change for us gulf and atlantic coasts role of hurricane frequency uncertainty

description: This study links physics-based projections of hurricanes under climate change to a power outage risk model for the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts, to see what drives uncertainty in future outage risk. Negin Alemazkoor, Benjamin Rachunok, Daniel Chavas and Roshanak Nateghi of Purdue University, Andrea Staid of Sandia National Laboratories and Arghavan Louhghalam and Mazdak Tootkaboni of the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth published it in Scientific Reports in September 2020. Simulated storms feed an outage model that estimates the fraction of people losing power, aggregated over four regions, the Gulf, upper Atlantic, lower Atlantic and Florida, and a polynomial chaos method propagates the uncertainty efficiently. Uncertainty in the frequency of weaker storms explains more than 95 percent of the uncertainty in outage projections, and the expected annual share of affected customers varies widely. Coverage is the US hurricane coast. Format and access: open article with supplementary information; code and data are available on request. Licence: CC-BY-4.0; free. Caveats: results depend on the outage model and on the storm projection ensemble. It supports climate adaptation, hazard exposure and resilience planning for grids facing hurricanes. A related catalogue record is the benchmark of hurricane outage models across 1,910 US cities.
